articles.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
articles.summary: Sotheby's says it will work with the heirs of a family who had previously owned the artwork to try and reach a solution.
articles.body:
Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.

Châtaigniers en Fleurs, which carries an estimate of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.

But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - earlier German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Sotheby's say its own "extensive research" has not established this, but say they will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," Sotheby's told the BBC in a statement.

"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."

The painting - whose name translates as Blossoming Chestnut Trees - is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.

Four other owners have had it since before it was put up for auction this year.

Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times , has written to Sotherby's.

He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

articles.title: US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
articles.summary: Sean Duffy, the country’s transportation secretary, said his agency is ‘going to hold people accountable’.
articles.body:
The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that halted all air traffic inside the country.

At a news conference in Washington, DC, on Saturday, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy spoke about routine maintenance that was performed on Friday to upgrade a router from copper to fibre at a “very remote location”.

Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router in question to start flooding other ones in the country’s air traffic control system.

“We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters at the Department of Transportation.

When those connection issues caused disruption in radar feeds and communications between air traffic controllers and aeroplanes, Duffy said a ground stop was ordered.

“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” he said.

The Transportation Department identified the contractor of Friday’s maintenance as L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company that has been tasked with modernising the communications system for the FAA.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”.

“They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

In response to Duffy’s allegations, L3Harris told Al Jazeera it has been working “in close coordination with the FAA” and places safety and reliability as its “highest priorities”.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” a spokesperson for the company said. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

Amid concerns that Friday’s ground stop was the result of a cyberattack, the US government said Saturday it did not “believe” that was the cause.

“Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said. “So, we don’t believe this was cyber at all.”

The head of the FAA, who also spoke at Saturday’s news conference, echoed the transportation secretary’s remarks, saying the system outage was caused by an equipment error.

“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said.

A root cause analysis would be shared with the public when it is available, he added.

As airlines and thousands of travellers begin the process of digging out from Friday’s groundstop, the longest and only second nationwide stop since 9/11, the FAA said full schedule integrity is expected by the end of Sunday.

“We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.”

Bedford said the FAA expects about 4,000 to 5,000 flights out of the 41,000 scheduled on Saturday to be cancelled.

“That will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” he said. “I do think the worst is behind us.”

articles.title: A Connecticut teacher suspended for refusing to remove a classroom crucifix displayed for 10 years sues school district over First Amendment rights; appeals court weighs religious expression vs school speech
articles.summary: A Connecticut public school teacher who was suspended after refusing to remove a crucifix from her classroom is taking her First Amendment battle to a
articles.body: A Connecticut public school teacher who was suspended after refusing to remove a crucifix from her classroom is taking her First Amendment battle to a federal appeals court. Marisol Arroyo-Castro, who had displayed the religious symbol near her desk for nearly a decade, is challenging a school district’s decision to remove it. The case is scheduled for oral arguments on December 7, 2026.Arroyo-Castro taught middle-school social studies at DiLoreto Elementary & Middle School in New Britain, Connecticut. She said the crucifix was a personal expression of her faith and a source of comfort during her working day. However, school administrators instructed her to take it down, warning that refusing to comply could lead to disciplinary action.The disagreement escalated in December 2024, when the teacher was reprimanded for insubordination. The school district subsequently removed the crucifix and suspended her for two days without pay. She was later placed on paid administrative leave and reassigned to a non-teaching position in March 2025.Teacher says crucifix was a personal expression of faithArroyo-Castro said the crucifix had been displayed near her desk for approximately 10 years. She described it as something that helped her remain calm while grading papers and completing other classroom work.“I pretty much kept it to myself,” she said, explaining that the symbol was a personal source of comfort.She recalled becoming emotional when administrators told her to remove it. According to her account, she was informed that she could return to her classroom only if she left the crucifix behind.“I said, ‘I can't,’” she recalled.On December 11, 2024, Arroyo-Castro received a formal reprimand for insubordination. The following day, the school removed the crucifix and suspended her for two days without pay. On December 16, she was placed on paid administrative leave. In March 2025, she was reassigned to a role that did not involve teaching students.“They suspended me,” she told Fox News Digital. “Then they told me that they were going to pay me after that, but that I couldn't go back into the school near the children, that they didn't want me around the students, that I'm not supposed to talk to the students or interact with them or any of the staff in the school.”Federal appeals court to hear teacher's First Amendment caseArroyo-Castro filed a federal lawsuit in January 2025, alleging that the school district had violated her First Amendment rights by restricting her religious expression.In November 2025, a federal judge denied her request for a preliminary injunction, ruling that she was unlikely to succeed because the crucifix display constituted government speech. The teacher subsequently appealed the decision to the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.Her legal team is arguing that the crucifix represented private religious expression rather than an endorsement of religion by the school.Becky Rees Dummermuth, senior counsel at First Liberty Institute, which is representing Arroyo-Castro, said the appeal would focus on the protection afforded to teachers' private religious expression under the First Amendment.“So we've appealed to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, and in the next couple of weeks, on Dec. 7, we'll have an oral argument there in the Second Circuit Court of Appeals in New York City, and we'll argue before the court that Marisol's speech was private speech,” she told Fox News Digital.Dummermuth also referred to the US Supreme Court's 2022 decision in the case involving former high school football coach Joe Kennedy, whose post-game prayers became the subject of a legal dispute.The attorney said the case supported the argument that public school employees do not automatically lose their right to private religious expression at work. First Liberty is relying on the First Amendment's Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses in its challenge.School district says dispute involved more than the crucifixThe Consolidated School District of New Britain has defended its actions, maintaining that the dispute involved concerns beyond the presence of a religious symbol in the classroom.In a statement to Fox News Digital, the district said its concerns related to a broader pattern of statements and actions involving students from different religious backgrounds.“The Consolidated School District of New Britain has consistently maintained that this matter extends beyond the presence of a religious symbol in a classroom. As outlined in the attached independent, third-party investigative report, the district's concerns involved a broader pattern of statements and actions that raised serious concerns about the treatment of students of differing religious backgrounds.”The district said it had offered Arroyo-Castro several ways to practise her faith without affecting the religious freedoms of her students, but that she and her attorneys had declined those options.It also said it had a responsibility to ensure that classrooms remained inclusive and welcoming to students and families from different faiths.The district referred to an independent investigative report that included interviews with four teachers, the principal, the assistant principal and Arroyo-Castro. The report documented claims by some students that the teacher had referred to God, Jesus and religion in ways the investigator considered inappropriate. Arroyo-Castro denied making such references during class.Teachers interviewed during the investigation also raised concerns about her classroom management and interactions with students.First Liberty disputes school district's explanationFirst Liberty Institute has challenged the district's account, arguing that administrators had told Arroyo-Castro she could return to her classroom if she removed the crucifix.“The school district repeatedly told Ms. Castro that she could return to the classroom if she simply took down the crucifix. When they removed her from the classroom, the only concern they mentioned was preventing an alleged Establishment Clause violation, a baseless concern that cannot survive the Supreme Court's Kennedy decision,” the organisation said.The school district, however, maintains that its decisions were based on its responsibility to protect students' religious freedoms and provide an inclusive learning environment.The Second Circuit hearing on December 7 will consider Arroyo-Castro's appeal against the denial of her request for preliminary relief. The dispute centres on whether the crucifix was protected private religious expression or a classroom display that the school could regulate.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Built around 1870, the 90-foot-tall structure was originally part of the area's water supply infrastructure. By the time Russell and Jannette Harris purchased it in 1997, the tower had fallen into disuse.Russell, a former television presenter and producer, had admired the building for years before deciding to buy it. However, turning a Victorian water tower into a comfortable family home proved far more complicated than the couple initially imagined.According to The Times, the renovation involved architect Julian Baker of Ellis Williams Architects and took seven years to complete. The project, initially budgeted at £150,000, eventually cost approximately £830,000. Work began in 2002, and the family moved into their new home in the summer of 2004. Rather than demolishing the historic structure or concealing its unusual shape, the architects designed a sweeping modern extension around the original octagonal tower. The result was a striking contrast between Victorian stonework and contemporary glass, steel and minimalist interiors.Inside the five-bedroom propertySpread across 6,127 square feet, the house has five bedrooms, four bathrooms and several spaces designed for both family life and entertaining. The main living area is arranged across different levels, allowing the kitchen, dining and sitting spaces to remain connected without losing their individual character. Large glass panels bring natural light into the rooms and open up views of the surrounding countryside.The principal bedroom occupies a double-height space with a mezzanine bathroom. Elsewhere, the house includes a winter lounge, a dedicated home office, a cinema room, a gym and a sauna. One of the property's most memorable features is its rooftop garden, positioned approximately 80 feet above ground. An eight-person teak hot tub sits at the top, offering panoramic views stretching across Cheshire towards Manchester, Liverpool, North Wales and the Peak District.The outdoor areas are equally carefully planned. Landscaped gardens surround the building, while a Japanese koi pond sits beside a breakfast terrace positioned to catch the morning sun. A separate rear terrace overlooks open countryside.An award-winning transformationThe restoration did more than create an unusual family residence. It also attracted attention from the architectural world. Lymm Water Tower received several honours, including a Royal Institute of British Architects award in 2006. It was also a finalist in the 2006 Grand Designs Awards and was selected by television presenter Kevin McCloud among his favourite 100 projects.The renovation was documented in the television series Seven-Year Makeover, giving viewers an insight into the challenges of adapting a protected historic building for modern use. Over the years, the Harrises also began welcoming paying guests, renting out part of the property through Airbnb after their children grew older.A £3 million home with an unusual income streamBeyond its architecture, the property offers something rarely associated with a family home: an established source of rental income. Telecommunications companies lease space within the upper section of the tower for communications equipment. According to the current property listing, these arrangements generate approximately £75,000 annually, although the income would remain subject to the relevant lease agreements and costs.The house was previously marketed for £2.5 million in 2016, but a sale did not materialise. It returned to the market in August 2026, this time with an asking price of offers over £3 million. After more than two decades of living in the converted landmark, Russell and Jannette Harris are now looking to move on. For the next owner, the property offers more than an unconventional address. It is a piece of Victorian engineering history that has spent the past two decades serving an entirely different purpose: being a family home.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Tens of thousands march in latest Portugal housing protests
articles.summary: These were the biggest protests against rising housing costs in Portugal since the social movement began weeks ago.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of more than 30 towns and cities in Portugal to protest against surging rental prices, demanding urgent government action to address the country’s worsening housing crisis.

Organised by the Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) platform, demonstrations on Saturday took place under the slogan “They will not steal our right to a home,” with protests in Lisbon, Porto, Faro, Portimao, Coimbra, Braga and other locations. It was the biggest national demonstration since the social movement began weeks ago .

Participants, ranging from teenagers to retired people, walked behind large banners, with the Lisbon march punctuated by drums, music, and chanting. Protesters called for caps to be placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing. They also demanded the reversal of proposed changes to rental legislation.

One woman on a protest march in Lisbon told Al Jazeera that she was a business owner, “and I can’t afford a house.”

“I can’t say much more than this. I’m forty-years-old, I can’t go to a bank and just buy a house with my money,” she added.

Another woman told Al Jazeera that she had joined the march to protest “for a better life, for all of us, not just the young people, all of us, because we deserve to have a home.”

One man told Al Jazeera “we have been suffering this for the last three or four years, and I have many friends and family in this situation, they had to move because they cannot afford the rent. If you earn, for example, a thousand euros, and you have to pay rent of six hundred, seven hundred, then you cannot live, it’s impossible.”

Casa Para Vivir brings together approximately 100 housing associations and grassroots organisations, is seeking tighter regulation on rental contracts, short-term tourist accommodation, and vacant properties.

The protests come after parliament approved the government’s proposed changes to provide greater flexibility in rental contracts and accelerate eviction procedures.

Housing campaigners warned the changes could weaken tenant protections amid rising rents and limited housing availability.

House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes in recent years, statistics show. Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61 percent, followed by the Netherlands with 34 percent, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week.

There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, property prices rose by almost 20 percent, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month.

Rental prices, too, have climbed significantly, recording a 68 percent increase since 2020, according to the government. Much of this jump in real estate costs has been fuelled by foreign buyers and investment funds, as the country’s relaxed climate near the ocean has attracted many remote workers and retirees.

The government has responded to the protests by lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals, and promising to build 145,000 new homes, but it acknowledged that the effects will not be immediate, as Prime Minister Luis Montenegro was urged by Casa Para Viver representatives to engage directly with them.

The protests in Portugal in recent weeks took their cue from demonstrations in neighbouring Spain last month over similar issues around housing and forced evictions . A wave of youth-led protests has swept Europe in the latter half of this year , with demonstrators across the continent denouncing rising prices and a lack of future prospects.

articles.summary: A 33-year-old woman from Nashville, Tennessee, has found an unconventional way to begin a new chapter after the end of her 10-year marriage — by bringing
articles.body: A 33-year-old woman from Nashville, Tennessee, has found an unconventional way to begin a new chapter after the end of her 10-year marriage — by bringing home a pet pig she had always wanted. Gayla Thompson adopted Daisy, an eight-week-old piglet weighing just nine pounds, in November 2025, after her divorce was finalized. She said getting the animal was a way of doing something for herself after years of being told she could not keep a pig.“My ex-husband always told me I couldn’t have a pet pig,” Thompson said to the New York Post. “So when the divorce was settled, getting my dream pig was the best way to start my new life.”Thompson jokingly said: "I traded one pig for another".Daisy has since grown considerably and now weighs around 50 pounds. She lives inside Thompson’s home, where she has her own bed, toys and litter box.The pig has also become a familiar sight at local shops. Thompson said she takes Daisy out on a leash, and employees at a nearby pet store have grown fond of her. She is also a regular visitor at pet store Sonic, where she sometimes gets a treat.Thompson, who has been involved in rescuing and rehabilitating animals since childhood, said caring for Daisy had been easier than she initially expected. She did, however, have to make changes around the house after the pig learnt to open cabinets.Her basic food and care expenses come to around $50 a month during winter, although she expects costs to decrease when Daisy moves into a specially built outdoor pen.Thompson's new partner is supportive of her plans and sometimes takes Daisy to his country property, where the pig can roam. The couple have also adopted another pig, named Dude. The two are now planning to build a small hobby farm, with chickens and possibly a donkey.For Thompson, the animals represent more than just a new hobby. They are part of the fresh start she wanted after her divorce. “This is my dream and I’m finally living it,” she said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: More than 100,000 rally across France in new Yellow Vest protests
articles.summary: Protesters chanted against declining affordability, the Macron government, police violence and poor school conditions.
articles.body:
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France in another round of cost-of-living rallies organised by the “Yellow Vests” and various youth movements.

Saturday’s protests saw a decline in turnout compared with previous weekends and stayed largely calm, authorities said.

The Ministry of the Interior reported that 106,000 people took part in protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris – down from 146,000 people nationwide and 46,000 in Paris last week. Student unions place Saturday’s protest numbers higher, at 200,000 people, including almost 100,000 in the capital.

The country has been gripped by high-school blockades, mass demonstrations, and strikes for more than a month, with protesters rallying against falling educational standards, cost-of-living increases, low wages, and police violence.

A number of demonstrators also carried signs targeting President Emmanuel Macron, who has faced significant criticism from protesters.

Some rallies in recent weeks have seen violence at the fringes, and the first major protest on October 17 saw looting in cities across France. Since then, police presence at rallies and controls on transport and permits to protest have been expanded.

Marseille, France’s second-largest city, banned protests over the weekend, but the prefecture announced that some 3,500 people still took to the streets. Local media reported that tear gas and a water cannon were used against protesters and shared images of fires burning in a popular local square.

In Lyon, local media reported that roughly 8,000 people took to the streets. They shared images of masked protesters chanting in front of fires lit in the street and police charging and using tear gas.

Tear gas use was also reported in Nantes, Bordeaux and Paris.

Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as “crumbs”.

If the demonstrations go ahead, they will take place on the eighth anniversary of the Gilet Jaune – which translates to “Yellow Vest” in French – movement, which rocked the beginning of the Macron government in 2018 with two years of protests triggered by rising fuel prices.

On Tuesday, the Yellow Vests will “celebrate their eight years where it all started: on roundabouts and toll booths all over France”, Yellow Vest protest tracking website 17octobregiletjaune.net writes.

articles.title: Kentucky coach Mark Pope gives insanely tone-deaf answer after Wildcats nearly lose as 30-point favorites
articles.summary: Mark Pope told Rupp Arena fans he hopes they "had fun" after Kentucky needed a near-miracle to escape Northern Arizona 78-77 as 30-point favorites.
articles.body: With all the upheaval caused by the FAA ground stop on Friday evening, it's easy to forget there were plenty of intriguing sporting events taking place to provide an appetizer to a weekend of great football. For example, college basketball is now in full swing and one game between a perennial power and a winless mid-major gave everyone a surprisingly drama-filled ending. The Kentucky Wildcats are one of the bluest bloods in the sport, but their season was already off to a shaky start coming into Friday's matchup with the Northern Arizona Lumberjacks. Big Blue Nation has already had to endure a scare against James Madison and a 20-point beatdown at the hands of the Kansas Jayhawks, but nothing could have prepared these Wildcat fans for what was to come in Rupp Arena against an 0-3 NAU squad. My buddy Dan Zaksheske wrote an entire piece about the game itself, so check that out if you're interested, but suffice to say, Kentucky needed a near-miracle to escape against the visiting Lumberjacks. What's worse, the Wildcats were 30-point favorites against Northern Arizona; this was supposed to be a "get right" game. Instead, Kentucky needed a couple of front-end misses from a pair of one-and-one opportunities at the free throw line from its opponent and some Rupp magic to squeak out a 78-77 "victory." COLLEGE BASKETBALL PLAYER'S BIZARRE FOUL SHOT GOES VIRAL IN SEASON-OPENER: 'DIABOLICAL' It hardly felt like a win to all the fans in attendance, and just as the loyal folks of Big Blue Nation were trying to make sense of what just happened, the most tone-deaf man in America was giving a postgame news conference. "I hope everyone in Rupp had fun." IS IT WEIRD FOR A COACH TO NOT TALK TO HIS TEAM AFTER A GAME, OR IS IT EXTREMELY WEIRD? Are you insane? For context, that man is Mark Pope, head basketball coach for the University of Kentucky. If you thought maybe that was the Northern Arizona coach, you would be forgiven, because in no world should a coach at a royally blue-blooded program like Kentucky ever say something like that after his $20 million roster just got worked by a mid-major. He's lucky they didn't fire him right after the presser was over. KENTUCKY COACH WILL STEIN TELLS WILDCATS PLAYERS 'IF YOU DON'T BELIEVE IN WHAT WE'RE DOING, YOU ARE HIGH' "It's really entertaining," he said, without a hint of irony. "I think this will be a fun team to follow." Yeah, for Tennessee, Florida, Arkansas, and Louisville fans, maybe. But do you really think Wildcat supporters sat in the stands in Lexington last night and thought, "Man, I'm having a great time watching my eight-time national championship-winning program need a miracle to avoid what might be the worst loss in school history?" Naturally, Pope got cooked over an open flame for this answer by both Kentucky fans and rivals alike. I know I've been tough on Pope before, but stuff like this makes him hard to defend. Kentucky fans were ready to get rid of John Calipari every season he failed to make the Sweet 16 towards the end there. I imagine those days feel halcyon by comparison. After Pope's eventful spring, in which he lost out on top recruit Tyran Stokes and had a disastrous Q&A on social media, I suggested he lie low for a bit and do some soul-searching while the fanbase cooled down. articles.title: Drought slows state’s rabi sowing; deficit hits 5.4 lakh hectares
articles.summary: Maharashtra rabi sowing down 38% by Nov 12, with a 5.4 lakh hectare deficit as drought and low soil moisture push farmers toward gram and jowar.
articles.body: Pune: Maharashtra’s rabi sowing has fallen behind last year’s pace by 5.40 lakh hectares, with drought and inadequate soil moisture forcing farmers to delay cultivation or restrict sowing to fields with assured irrigation.According to state agriculture department data, sowing was completed on just 8.92 lakh hectares—out of the state’s average rabi area of 57.80 lakh hectares—as of Nov 12, compared with 14.32 lakh hectares during the same period last year, marking a nearly 38% year-on-year decline.State agriculture commissioner Suraj Mandhare told TOI, “Due to severe water scarcity and deficient retreating monsoon rains, rabi sowing in Maharashtra has been hampered. Farmers are prioritising jowar and chickpea (gram) over water-intensive wheat and sugar cane. Sowing activity is still going on and will continue until the end of Dec.”The major crop areas are gram (43%), jowar (30%), wheat (20%), and maize (8%), he said.“A reduction in area is expected for wheat. We are prioritising and promoting the economical use of available water and ensuring fodder availability by providing subsidised seeds for crops like jowar, maize, and gram,” added Mandhare, who is monitoring the situation closely.The significant gap highlights the impact of this year’s deficient rainfall and prolonged dry spells on the state’s winter cropping season.Although reservoirs, lakes, and wells had adequate water following the initial phase of the monsoon, the subsequent dry spell and inadequate retreating monsoon rainfall affected soil moisture. Consequently, several farmers have been unable to undertake sowing even where they had initially planned rabi cultivation.The shortfall is particularly concerning in drought-prone districts of Marathwada and western Maharashtra, where farmers depend heavily on residual soil moisture and limited well irrigation for winter crops.Crop-wise figures show that farmers are prioritising relatively less water-intensive crops. Rabi jowar sowing has reached around 3.16 lakh hectares, accounting for 21% of its average area, while gram cultivation stands at approximately 3.79 lakh hectares, or 15%. Maize has covered around 82,569 hectares (22%).Wheat, which requires assured irrigation at critical growth stages, has recorded particularly slow progress. Its sowing stands at just 53,626 hectares, barely 5% of the average area of 11.80 lakh hectares, officials said.Agricultural experts said the availability of soil moisture and assured irrigation would determine the final rabi acreage rather than the calendar alone. Farmers without sufficient water are increasingly reluctant to invest in crops that require multiple irrigations.“There is no soil moisture in several jowar-growing tehsils. We cannot even recommend sowing this season,” Solapur district agriculture officer S. Bhosale said, highlighting the worsening conditions in one of Maharashtra’s major rabi jowar belts.Agricultural universities have also advised farmers to prioritise low-water crops such as gram, rabi jowar, and safflower, and to undertake the cultivation of wheat and other irrigation-dependent crops only where protective irrigation is available during critical growth stages. They have recommended short-duration varieties and water-saving irrigation methods such as sprinklers and drip systems.The agriculture department, however, expects sowing activity to continue until the end of Dec.“The coming weeks will therefore be crucial in determining how much of the remaining average area can be brought under cultivation. However, it is expected to be significantly lower because there is no possibility of additional water,” said another senior agriculture official.Experts caution that delayed sowing could also affect crop productivity, particularly where farmers miss the optimum sowing window.“Even if additional sowing takes place in the coming weeks, the 5.40 lakh hectare gap compared with last year reflects the scale of the drought’s impact on Maharashtra’s rabi season,” added the official.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news.
